Metabolic Myopathies

Lecture Companion · Ben Barnes, MD · 31 lecture slides + supplied 2022 Continuum review

← Week 17Rapid-review Factoid →PatternSubtypesGlycogenFat OxidationMitochondriaDiagnosisTreatmentMastery

Learning objectives & the big picture

OFFICIAL LEARNING OBJECTIVES · SLIDE 3
  1. Appreciate clinical features common to different metabolic myopathies.
  2. Distinguish among subtypes of metabolic myopathy using clinical and diagnostic features.
  3. Recount associated treatment approaches.

Metabolic myopathies impair the ability of skeletal muscle to use energy substrates when activity increases demand for ATP. The most diagnostic question is not simply “Does exercise hurt?” but when does it hurt, what activity provokes it, and what happens between episodes?

Brief intense activity → glycogenolysis/glycolysis defects
Prolonged exercise or fasting → fatty acid oxidation defects
Energy stress + extra-muscular findings → mitochondrial disease

Use this timing-based approach to choose subsequent investigations. There is significant overlap, and genetic confirmation may be necessary.

1 · Recognize the myopathic pattern

Myopathies are disorders of skeletal muscle. Across etiologies, proximal weakness (raising the arms, standing from a chair, climbing stairs), exercise intolerance, fatigue and sometimes proximal pain are characteristic. The lecture emphasizes a normal sensory examination and generally normal reflexes, except in some long-standing dystrophies. Gait findings can include waddling, hyperlordosis, and knee locking.

MUST KNOW · WHAT MAKES A METABOLIC CAUSE LIKELY
  • Recurrent/relapsing exercise-associated cramps, weakness or myalgia, rather than a continually progressive fixed deficit.
  • Normal neurological examination between events is common.
  • Events provoked by activity, fasting, fever/illness.
  • Repeated rhabdomyolysis: myalgia/weakness, dark myoglobin-containing urine, CK >10× the upper limit of normal, possible kidney injury.

Do not assume every myopathy is metabolic

The lecture distinguishes inflammatory (dermatomyositis, polymyositis, necrotizing), genetic/structural (Duchenne/Becker, limb-girdle), toxic (steroids, alcohol, statins, colchicine), and metabolic conditions. A clinical history of exposure, fixed weakness, or persistent CK elevation can redirect the differential.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A patient has proximal weakness, normal sensation, and intact reflexes. What anatomical level is favored?

The pattern favors a muscle disorder rather than a sensory peripheral neuropathy; use the time course and triggers to narrow the etiology.

2 · Three substrate pathways, three patterns

Muscle changes its energy supply with exercise intensity and duration. Intense activity requires readily available carbohydrate metabolism; prolonged, lower-intensity work increasingly uses fatty acids; oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria is the downstream ATP-producing machinery for multiple substrates.

FeatureGlycogen storage / glycolyticFatty acid oxidationMitochondrial
Typical triggerSeconds–minutes of intense/sprint activityProlonged activity, fasting, illnessProlonged activity, fasting, illness
Prominent symptomsMuscle cramps, exercise intolerance; delayed rhabdomyolysisExercise-related myalgia, pigmenturia often delayedMyalgia/fatigue; possible fixed weakness and multisystem signs
Inter-episode examinationUsually normalUsually normalMay reveal ptosis, ophthalmoparesis, sensory/hearing/visual or other findings
Distinctive clueSecond wind particularly McArdle; sometimes goutAcylcarnitine abnormalities; hypoketotic hypoglycemia during crisesRagged red/COX-negative muscle fibers; lactate sometimes elevated
Inheritance cluesMost AR; some X-linked defectsTypically ARMaternal for mtDNA; nuclear defects may follow Mendelian patterns
COMMON CONFUSIONRhabdomyolysis occurs in all three major groups. Exercise duration and intensity, fasting/illness exposure, the second-wind phenomenon, and multisystem clues distinguish them better than dark urine alone.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why does a 30-second maximal effort favor a carbohydrate pathway disorder over a fatty acid oxidation defect?

Rapid high-intensity work depends heavily on glycogenolysis/glycolysis. Fatty acid oxidation contributes more during sustained exercise.

3 · Glycogen storage diseases: the sprint problem

These diseases block glycogenolysis or glycolysis, limiting prompt ATP supply for high-intensity muscle work. Symptoms often emerge within seconds to minutes of exercise or when intensity increases: cramps, exercise intolerance, pain, and sometimes delayed rhabdomyolysis.

McArdle disease (GSD V)

McArdle disease is due to pathogenic variants of PYGM, encoding skeletal-muscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase). The muscle cannot mobilize its stored glycogen effectively. Patients may discover a second wind: initial fatigue/cramping improves after easing activity, resting, and resuming at a lower intensity, when alternative circulating fuels are available.

HIGH YIELD · SECOND WINDA patient who cannot sustain the first few minutes of activity but can continue after reducing intensity and resting has a signature clue for McArdle disease. The provided review contrasts this with glycolytic disorders such as Tarui disease, which typically lack a second wind.

Other glycolytic defects

Tarui disease (GSD VII) is phosphofructokinase deficiency. The lecture lists phosphoglycerate kinase 1, phosphoglucomutase 1, phosphoglycerate mutase, lactate dehydrogenase, aldolase A, and beta-enolase deficiencies as further examples. They need not all be memorized to identical depth; focus on pathway and clinical timing.

Diagnostic reasoning

  • CK: may remain chronically elevated in McArdle disease; in many other glycogen storage diseases it normalizes between events.
  • Uric acid: can be elevated, leading to myogenic hyperuricemia/gout due to increased purine degradation during exercise.
  • Nonischemic forearm exercise test: minimal/no lactate rise with increased ammonia suggests impaired glycogenolysis/glycolysis.
  • Exercise stress testing: second wind favors McArdle; absent second wind can favor glycolytic defects/GSD9.
  • EMG/NCS: often normal between episodes; targeted genetic panels and, when needed, enzyme analysis help establish diagnosis.
FIRST AID CONNECTIONFirst Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (2025), biochemistry pp. 84–85: Skeletal-muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency causes glycogen accumulation with exercise-induced painful cramps and myoglobinuria. First Aid also highlights a flat lactate response during exercise while ammonia rises, and usually preserved blood glucose because the muscle-specific enzyme defect does not directly block hepatic glucose release.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A patient reports cramping immediately after sprinting, elevated CK between events, gout, and improvement after warming up. What diagnosis and enzyme defect fit?

McArdle disease (GSD V), due to deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase (PYGM).

4 · Fatty acid oxidation defects: the endurance/fasting problem

Short- and medium-chain fatty acids can enter the mitochondrial matrix without the long-chain carnitine shuttle, while long and very-long chains require the carnitine palmitoyltransferase transport system. A defect reduces access to a crucial fuel during fasting or prolonged exercise, when carbohydrate stores are no longer enough.

Lecture examples include CPT I/CPT II defects, carnitine–acylcarnitine translocase deficiency, VLCAD deficiency, medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, and primary carnitine deficiency. The reviewed group is predominantly autosomal recessive.

MUST KNOW · PRESENTATIONEndurance activity + fasting/illness → delayed muscle pain, pigmenturia, and rhabdomyolysis. Unlike the cramping of glycogen storage diseases, myalgia is especially typical here. CK is usually normal between attacks.

Diagnostic approach

  • Serum acylcarnitine profile: high-value test; more revealing during fasting or after exercise/acute attacks.
  • Urinary organic acids: dicarboxylic acid elevations may accompany beta-oxidation defects.
  • During decompensation: hypoketotic hypoglycemia can occur.
  • Muscle biopsy: may show increased neutral lipid, but can be normal (including in CPT II deficiency).
  • Genetic panels: confirm the candidate defect with clinical/metabolite context.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why can an acylcarnitine profile obtained during fasting outperform the same test when asymptomatic?

Fasting raises dependence on fatty acid oxidation and can amplify pathway-specific acylcarnitine accumulation.

5 · Mitochondrial myopathy: the energy-demand and multisystem problem

Mitochondrial defects can disrupt the electron transport chain or other components of mitochondrial metabolism. Because mitochondria are the common oxidative endpoint for carbohydrates, fatty acids, and many amino acids, impaired function can create broad ATP deficiency, particularly during high energy demand.

HIGH YIELD · MULTISYSTEM CLUESExercise intolerance with ptosis, ophthalmoparesis, hearing loss, visual symptoms, short stature, gastrointestinal symptoms, or neurological findings strongly raises the possibility of mitochondrial disease. The lecture describes occasional exercise-associated deafness, visual symptoms, abdominal pain, and vomiting.

Diagnostic clues and limitations

  • Serum lactate: may be elevated (lecture review: approximately 65% of cases), but normal lactate does not rule it out.
  • Alanine and urine organic acids: may be elevated; CK ranges from normal to chronically elevated.
  • Exercise testing: low VO₂max, high respiratory exchange ratio, disproportionate heart-rate/ventilatory response.
  • Muscle pathology: ragged red fibers, cytochrome c oxidase (COX)-negative fibers, and ultrastructural paracrystalline inclusions are useful clues.
  • DNA testing: sequencing of muscle-derived mtDNA may reveal mutations absent in blood due to tissue-specific heteroplasmy. Nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes can also be involved.
EXAM TRAPA negative blood mtDNA study does not exclude a mitochondrial disorder. Rapidly turning-over blood cells may contain much less pathogenic mitochondrial DNA than affected skeletal muscle.

The lecture’s diagnostic case

A 30-year-old man with recurrent rhabdomyolysis and a normal blood genetic panel had ragged red, COX-negative fibers on muscle biopsy. Sequencing muscle-derived DNA identified an MT-CYB variant with substantial mutant heteroplasmy that was not detectable in blood. This is the practical reason to consider biopsy and muscle DNA testing after a non-diagnostic peripheral workup.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A patient has exercise-related muscle symptoms, hearing impairment, ptosis and a normal blood mtDNA panel. What next investigation can still be diagnostic?

Muscle biopsy with relevant histology and muscle-derived mtDNA sequencing; blood testing can be falsely negative.

6 · Build a defensible diagnostic workup

Start with the trigger history (seconds vs prolonged activity, intensity, fasting, febrile illness), childhood exercise avoidance, pigmenturia episodes, family history, and a focused neurological exam. Separate proximal myopathic findings from sensory or motor-neuron disease and recognize the renal risk of an acute rhabdomyolysis episode.

Question / testWhy it helpsInterpretation / caution
CK and renal functionDocuments muscle injury and complicationsCK >10× ULN supports rhabdomyolysis; trend levels; monitor renal function and electrolytes
Nonischemic forearm exercise: lactate and ammoniaScreens glycogenolysis/glycolysisBlunted lactate + preserved/exaggerated ammonia rise points toward carbohydrate pathway defects
Acylcarnitines ± urine organic acidsEvaluates fatty acid utilizationCharacteristic profiles can direct genetic testing; timing matters
Lactate/alanine and graded exercise testEvaluates oxidative limitationElevated lactate/low VO₂max can support mitochondrial hypothesis; not specific alone
Next-generation sequencing panelsEstablishes molecular etiologyMatch genotype to phenotype and biochemical profile; variants of uncertain significance need validation
Muscle biopsyResolves unresolved casesAbsent phosphorylase, lipid excess, ragged-red/COX-negative fibers; muscle mtDNA when blood negative
CLINICAL CONNECTIONMyoglobinuria → acute tubular injury can complicate severe rhabdomyolysis. In the provided case, markedly elevated CK with oliguria/anuria and rising creatinine justified careful hydration and kidney monitoring. This is clinically more urgent than classifying the genetic subtype during the acute episode.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · In a patient with recurrent rhabdomyolysis, why are a normal exam and normal CK between episodes insufficient to exclude metabolic myopathy?

Some metabolic defects cause episodic failure only when ATP demand or metabolic stress exceeds capacity; resting muscle function may remain normal.

7 · Treatment follows the pathway

Across groups, the lecture emphasizes carefully progressive exercise rather than global inactivity, and individualized avoidance of triggers such as fasting, severe exertion, or illness-related metabolic stress. Dietary strategies and supplements vary by subtype, and review-article options should not be assumed equally proven.

CategoryCore lecture/review approachDistinctive reasoning
McArdle / glycogen storageGradual activity; pre-exercise sucrose or glucose in McArdle; assess/treat hyperuricemia; other review-listed therapies have variable evidenceCirculating sugar can bypass defective muscle glycogen mobilization.
Some glycolytic defectsReview lists overnight fasting for certain defects (e.g. phosphofructokinase deficiency)Do not generalize McArdle carbohydrate recommendations to Tarui disease; fasting response differs.
Fatty acid oxidationAvoid fasting and exercise during febrile illness; carbohydrate-rich dietary support; L-carnitine only with documented low levels; triheptanoin in selected severe cases depending on approvalReduce reliance on impaired fat oxidation during exertion.
MitochondrialCarefully progressive training; avoid fasting/illness exercise; review lists a mitochondrial cocktail such as coenzyme Q10/idebenone, α-lipoic acid, vitamin E, creatineSupport oxidative energy production; evidence varies by intervention.
COMMON CONFUSIONPre-exercise sugar is not a universal metabolic-myopathy prescription. In McArdle it may improve tolerance; in some glycolytic defects carbohydrate feeding can worsen exercise tolerance by suppressing alternative fatty-acid fuel availability. In fatty-acid oxidation defects, fasting avoidance and carbohydrate availability are central.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why might sugar before exercise help McArdle disease but not Tarui disease?

In McArdle, the block is at glycogen liberation, so circulating glucose can enter downstream glycolysis. In Tarui disease, the glycolytic pathway itself is impaired.

8 · Integrate: what the test writer wants you to notice

Patient A · Brief sprint

Cramps on high-intensity activity; improves after rest and lower intensity; recurrent gout; CK stays high.

Think: McArdle / PYGM / second wind.

Patient B · Endurance in fasting state

Prolonged cycling → delayed myalgia, tea-colored urine, normal interepisode CK.

Think: fatty acid oxidation defect; order acylcarnitines.

Patient C · Multiple systems

Exercise intolerance plus ptosis, hearing impairment and possible elevated lactate.

Think: mitochondrial dysfunction; evaluate muscle mtDNA if blood negative.

Patient D · A mimic

Persistent weakness and CK abnormality outside discrete exertional events; prior statin exposure or dystrophy findings.

Think: toxic/structural/pseudometabolic mimics.

MSK CONNECTIONThe Week 17 skeletal-muscle physiology lecture explains ATP demand, oxidative phosphorylation, glycolysis, and muscular fatigue. This lecture illustrates what happens when those ordinary energy pathways fail under different exercise conditions.
FIRST AID CONNECTIONFirst Aid 2025, biochemistry pp. 84–85: Muscle and liver differ in glycogen function. The classic McArdle presentation is muscle-specific exertional energy failure, with blood glucose generally spared—useful when differentiating it from glycogen storage disorders characterized by severe hepatic fasting hypoglycemia.

MASTER THESE BEFORE MOVING ON

  1. Time to symptom onset: early, high-intensity cramps → glycogen; sustained exercise/fasting → fat oxidation or mitochondria.
  2. McArdle’s unique logic: PYGM deficiency, second wind, chronic hyperCKemia, possible hyperuricemia.
  3. Laboratory localization: flat lactate rise → carbohydrate-pathway block; acylcarnitines → fatty acid oxidation; ragged red/COX-negative → mitochondria.
  4. Negative blood mtDNA is not definitive: heteroplasmy varies by tissue; muscle may reveal the diagnosis.
  5. Management differs: carbohydrates may help one disorder while being unhelpful or counterproductive in another.

THE MOST USEFUL FIRST AID CONNECTIONS

  1. McArdle (GSD V) → myophosphorylase defect → exertional cramps/myoglobinuria.
  2. Glycogen phosphorylase defect → little exercise-induced lactate rise with ammonia response preserved.
  3. Muscle-specific GSD V → normal systemic blood glucose contrasts with liver glycogen-storage phenotypes.
